claims.notes: THE FIRST SEASON OF THE HARBOUR WORKS, IN THE ENGINEER'S OWN REPORT — and it is the other end of the story the Democrat tells in August 1834, when the North Pier is being run across the sand-bar (1834-08-13, claim c001 there). What this says about the winter of 1833-34 is that ALMOST NOTHING HAD BEEN BUILT: no engineer officer could be spared, so the commanding officer at Fort Dearborn ran the work; materials and workmen could not be got; everything but timber and stone had to come from Buffalo; the first proposals were rejected as exorbitant; and when contracts were finally made they were for a small quantity of stone and timber. 'But little has been done' beyond collecting materials and constructing a small portion. FOR A RECONSTRUCTION STANDING IN 1835 THIS IS THE DATED FLOOR: the works begin here, essentially unbuilt in January 1834, and are a pier crossing the bar by August. Anything the scene shows at the river mouth has to sit between those two readings. The lines are interleaved with the political column beside them and the four named here are the ones the report can be followed through; three inside the range (483, 485) are single stray words and are excluded.

entities.role: author of the dedication hymn, of this place

claims.notes: A CHURCH BUILDING IS DEDICATED IN CHICAGO IN JANUARY 1834, and the paper prints the order of service and the hymn written for it. This is a BUILDING claim before it is anything else: 'we dedicate this house to Thee, to Thee these hallowed walls we raise' is a finished structure with walls, opened for worship eighteen months before the scene date — so the Presbyterian meeting house stands in 1835 and the reconstruction has a date for when it started standing. It is corroborated one week later as a working public room: the Chicago Temperance Society meets at 'the Presbyterian Meeting house, 6 o'clock P.M.' on 30 January (1834-01-28, claim c002 there). WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED is where it stood, how big it was or what it was built of; none of that is in the notice, and none of it is supplied. G. N. Sproat, who wrote the hymn, is named 'of this place' and is minted as a resident.

claims.notes: A SECOND BUSINESS AT THE DEMOCRAT'S OWN CORNER. W. Kimball's New Store is on the corner of South Water and Clark streets — the same corner the paper's imprint gives for the building it is printed in (1834-01-07, claim c006) — so that corner carries at least two addresses in January 1834 and is the busiest documented intersection in this reading pass. The stock is the general assortment of the period, and the terms are the frontier's: cash OR country produce. The advertisement is repeated verbatim in the following issue (1834-01-28, page 4, lines 1005-1009), where the corner reads whole.

claims.notes: A LOT IN THE SCHOOL SECTION, BY BLOCK NUMBER — Block 120, Lot 3 — offered in January 1834 and still offered in August (1834-08-13, page 3 column 4). This is the school section, section 16, being sold off lot by lot through the town's own newspaper, and it is a plat-level placement of the kind the corpus rarely yields. Nothing here says anything is BUILT on it; the claim is a parcel on the market, which is what the south-west quarter of this town largely was in 1834.

claims.notes: HAY IS BEING CUT AND SOLD SIX MILES OUT, and enquiry is made of a man three miles south of the town. Two distances from the town centre in one small advertisement, which is the sort of thing a reconstruction of the ground BEYOND the plat has almost nothing else of: prairie hay as a traded crop within a morning's haul, and a settler established three miles south by January 1834. B. Jones, the town agent for it, is the same forwarding and commission merchant whose own advertisement runs in this month's issues.

claims.notes: A DEATH IN THE FRENCH TRADING COMMUNITY. John B. Chevallier is dead by January 1834 and Louis P. Chevallier is settling the estate through the Cook County probate court. The Chevalliers belong to the older, pre-town population of this place, which the reconstruction has to represent alongside the Yankee merchants filling the advertising columns — and this is the kind of record that says such a family was still here, still holding property, at the moment the town incorporated. The date printed as '1844' is read 1834 from the notice's own 'Jan. 15' and from the issue it stands in; the OCR's '1844' is a recognition error and is bracketed.
